doc.title: Bill Mays interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 5, 2025

title: What he wants from bass players
summary: He wants good intonation, bow, reading and dialogue, lists bassists he has played with, and says drugs or drink spoil time.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: It was a great statement. Let’s talk about bass players. The reason I went that direction is because that last little piano excerpt I played you had taken – your left hand became a walking bass. And over the years I’m sure you’ve worked with many bass players, sometimes by choice, sometimes by circumstance. What do you like or not like to get from a bassist?

Well I want them to be in tune, I want them to be just a tiny, tiny bit on top of the beat generally. I want them to be able to play with the bow because I use arco in a lot of my presentations. They need to be good readers some of the time, if it’s a project that requires that and then I’ve played with bass players who weren’t good readers but had tremendous ears. I want them to be supportive and contributive. I want them to be able to just play time and keep it really basic sometimes, and then I want them to know when I want them to dialogue with me. And I’ve played with such a wide variety of bass players who had such different sounds and feels and approaches from Ron Carter to Ron McClure, Red Mitchell to Ray Drummond, Martin Wind to Dean Johnson, Tommy Cecil, Todd Coolman. I’m leaving out dozens of bass players that I’ve played with and love but I’m trying to make a point, that I’ve learned from all of them. That ability to walk bass for oneself, I was scared to death of that fifty years ago. But when I moved to New York and played duo music a lot of the time because of the confines of the club or the budget or whatever it was, that gave me both the courage and the ability to accompany myself in a solo situation walking bass lines. It’s tricky because my right hand is going to lay a little bit behind the beat and hopefully my left hand walking the bass is going to be just right in the middle or a little bit on top so we don’t drag and slow way down. That’s what’s comfortable for me. But what was the question?
Well you know we were just talking about the difference from one bassist to the next. And you know what? What don’t you want the bass player to do?
Get high or drink. I won’t name names but I had to fire one, the only person I had to let go due to drug use. And then there were others that drank or smoked too much and the

time always came down and that’s a drag. Nothing is worse when you’re playing duo or trio if the time is not in the pocket. If it’s rushing or it’s dragging it’s just a drag. There ain’t no rush to it.
Yeah. And you know, and so that’s requirement number one. And yeah I guess I answered that question.
